SF.summary:
- **De’Zhaun Stribling** — San Francisco’s top 2026 draft pick was viewed by PFF as a major reach, though his physical style, blocking, and vertical-threat traits fit Kyle Shanahan’s system. The value question matters because he could be pushed into a role sooner than the draft slot suggests. [1]

- **Carver Willis** — The 49ers added the offensive lineman for depth and run-blocking help, but PFF flagged him as the class’s biggest reach after taking him at No. 127 despite a much lower pre-draft ranking. That makes him a developmental piece to watch in camp rather than a sure 2026 contributor. [1]

- **Running back group** — Shanahan’s history at running back is getting renewed scrutiny after another high draft investment at the position. The big question is whether this latest back can avoid the recent pattern of underwhelming 49ers RB picks. [4]

- **Jauan Jennings** — The former 49ers receiver is again being linked to the Seahawks after Seattle previously surfaced as a possible landing spot. His run-blocking and physical play would fit a run-first offense, but his next team is still not specified. [5]

- **Kyle Shanahan** — He drew criticism for the 49ers’ draft process and defended it by saying he evaluates prospects through a condensed February window with curated film from assistants. That keeps the spotlight on whether San Francisco’s internal grading can keep producing hits despite consensus skepticism. [6]

DEN.summary:
- **Jonah Coleman** — The rookie running back is part of a likely three-man rotation with J.K. Dobbins and RJ Harvey, and Denver could lean into that to protect Dobbins. That gives Coleman a real path to early touches, especially if he pushes Harvey on passing downs. [1, 6]

- **Justin Joly** — Denver passed on an earlier tight end but still targeted Joly, whom ESPN’s Jeremy Fowler said the Broncos liked as a pass-catching weapon. He could see situational work because Evan Engram’s health is a concern and the tight end room is unsettled. [1, 5]

- **Tyler Onyedim** — The Broncos’ top pick has a clear early role available at defensive tackle after John Franklin-Myers’ departure. He could start on early downs and rotate with Sai’vion Jones, with more snaps available if Denver uses a six-man interior rotation. [1, 3]

- **Red Murdock** — The rookie linebacker’s best chance to contribute is on special teams, with Denver’s linebacker rotation and established depth limiting defensive snaps. If injuries hit, he could get a look, but a year-one defensive role is not specified. [1, 3]

- **Casey** — Denver brought him in to develop at left guard as a future starter, but barring injuries he does not have a clear path to offensive snaps this season. His immediate value is likely tied to special teams and Ben Powers availability. [1]

JAX.summary:
- **Jaguars draft class** — The team’s 2026 draft was built around a roster that was viewed as having no clear holes, letting Jacksonville lean into best-player-available choices rather than forcing needs. That supports the idea that the class was designed for long-term depth more than immediate fixes. [3]

- **Liam Coen** — Jacksonville’s draft choices fit the head coach’s push for a tougher, more physical identity after last season’s 13-4 AFC South title run. What’s next is whether that edge shows up again on the field, especially after the team fell short of its ultimate goal. [4]

- **Nate Boerkircher** — The Jaguars used their top offseason asset on the Texas A&M tight end, and the early read is that he can fill a hybrid role with in-line blocking and detached usage. That matters because the tight end room appears open enough for a rookie to carve out snaps quickly. [5]

- **Hunter Long** — Boerkircher’s arrival puts pressure on Long, who played the second-most tight end snaps for Jacksonville last year at 41%. If Boerkircher earns a real role, Long’s usage could shrink. [5]

- **Johnny Mundt** — Mundt also logged a meaningful 36% of the tight end snaps last season, so Boerkircher’s addition creates another direct competition for playing time. The depth chart at tight end looks much less settled now. [5]

- **Trent Baalke** — Cleveland’s hiring of the former Jaguars GM as a consultant adds another layer to the Jaguars-Browns storyline, especially given Jacksonville’s Travis Hunter trade with Cleveland. The matchup now carries some front-office and draft history beyond the field. [6]

- **Keyron Crawford** — The Raiders added the edge rusher in the third round after already bolstering the defensive line with Kwity Paye in free agency. That deepens an already crowded front and suggests Crawford may have to earn his snap share in a rotation. [5, 6]

His versatility could help him compete for early special-teams and depth-chart work, though his exact role is not specified. [3]

- **Dave Merritt** — Reid addressed the defensive backs coach’s misdemeanor domestic battery charge, and Merritt remained with the team during rookie minicamp. The legal situation is still active, so this remains a storyline to watch around the staff. [1]
